text_blocks.snippet: You likely need a new roof in Utah [Highlight start] if your roof is near the end of its expected lifespan (roughly 15–20 years for three-tab asphalt, 20–30 years for architectural asphalt, and 40–70 years for metal) or shows widespread damage from intense UV rays, heavy snow loads, and freeze-thaw cycles [Highlight end] .

list.snippet: Curling, cracking, or buckling shingles: Often worst on sun-exposed south- and west-facing slopes or after heavy snow and freeze-thaw cycles.
Heavy granule loss: Dark, sandy granules collecting in gutters or at the base of downspouts mean the protective surface is wearing away.
Missing shingles or worn flashing: Wind, hail, or dried-out seals around chimneys, vents, and valleys leave vulnerable entry points.
Sagging rooflines or decking: A dip or "smile" along the ridge or slope can point to rotted decking, trapped moisture, or heavy snow strain.
Daylight coming through the roof boards: Any light visible in the attic means moisture can get in too.
Water stains, damp rafters, or soft decking: Dark marks, peeling paint, or soft spots on the underside of the roof deck signal past or ongoing leaks.
Moss or mold growth: Indicates trapped moisture and potential underlying rot.

text_blocks.snippet: When Replacement Makes More Sense Than Repair

list.snippet: Damage is spread across the roof rather than limited to one isolated spot.
You need repeated repairs after storms .
The roof already has multiple shingle layers and is aging out.

text_blocks.snippet: In Utah, a full tear-off and replacement generally requires a local building permit before work starts. For details on contracts and permitting, see Rock Solid Utah .
If you share your roof material and approximate age, I can help you weigh whether a repair , restoration, or full replacement makes more sense.
